approachQuestion.prompt:
Common Tolerance
Each of m nonempty nondecreasing arrays gives acceptable settings for one instrument. Find the narrowest closed integer interval [L,R] containing at least one setting from every array. Minimize R−L, then L. Example: [[1,8,12],[4,9],[6,10]] → [8,10]; [[2],[2,3]] → [2,2].

2 ≤ m ≤ 100000; total length N ≤ 300000. Values are signed 32-bit integers, and width uses 64-bit arithmetic. Arrays are read-only. Return just two endpoints. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 2 ≤ m ≤ 100000; total length N ≤ 300000. Values are signed 32-bit integers, and width uses 64-bit arithmetic. Arrays are read-only. Return just two endpoints.

options.text: Keep one entry from every array in a min-heap and track their current maximum. Record their interval; then remove the minimum and advance only its array, updating the maximum and candidate interval. Stop when the removed minimum has no successor. Compare widths and then left endpoints.
options.feedback: For a fixed current minimum, advancing any other array cannot raise that minimum or lower the maximum. Advancing its own array explores the next useful boundary; once it is exhausted no later boundary can cover all arrays.

options.text: Use the same frontier progression, but find its minimum by scanning all m current entries each time.
options.feedback: All candidates are considered correctly, but the repeated minimum scans are removable.

options.text: Take the minimum first entry as L and the maximum first entry as R and stop.
options.feedback: For [[1,8],[7,9]], this returns [1,7] although [7,8] is narrower.

options.text: Advance whichever array currently supplies the maximum.
options.feedback: For [[1,8],[7,9]], advancing 7 to 9 while leaving 1 cannot discover [7,8].

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A with a binary min-heap of m entries, bottom-up construction, and one scalar maximum. Let N be total input elements and m arrays; all are nonempty. Endpoints and width comparisons are constant-time. No input copies beyond current entries. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(N log(m+1)) time, O(m) auxiliary space
O(N log(m+1)) time, O(N) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: One head per array bounds memory while frontier repairs account for traversal time.
details: Initialization costs O(m); at most N entries are removed or inserted. Inputs with long interleaved arrays force a linear number of frontier repairs at height log m, so O(N log(m+1)) is tight in the worst case. One entry per array uses O(m) space. The maximum never decreases when the minimum advances and needs only one scalar.
“O(Nm) time, O(m) auxiliary space”: That is the repeated-scan frontier cost, not the heap implementation.
“O(N log(m+1)) time, O(N) auxiliary space”: The method never copies all N settings; it retains only m current settings.
“O(N) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The frontier requires m entries and heap mutations are not constant-time.
